facts.text: Carousels developed from knightly exercises at European courts, in which riders on horseback tested their skill by aiming a lance at small rings hung in the air.
The word carousel is usually traced to Italian and Spanish words (garosello, carosella) meaning little war.
To practice the ring game, people built a device with wooden seats hung from a central pole; it turned in a circle past an arm that held rings.
Early carousels were turned by human or horse power, which limited their size.
Beginning in the 1860s, carousels were driven by steam engines; electric motors were introduced later, around 1915, allowing larger and more elaborate rides.
American carousels, often called merry-go-rounds, turn counterclockwise, while in England they turn clockwise and are called roundabouts.
From 1885 onward, merry-go-rounds were a popular attraction at seaside resorts, amusement parks, public parks, fairs, and carnivals.
Many carousels kept a ring game: riders reached for rings as they passed, and a rider who caught the brass ring won a free ride.
